title: Equality, Identity, and Comparison
learningObjectives: Distinguish equality of values from identity of objects or storage.
Recognize that comparison operators may have type-specific behavior.
Explain why comparing composite structures can differ from comparing primitives.
Identify risks from coercive or case-sensitive comparisons.
Choose the comparison rule that matches the program's intent.

understand.concept: Equality asks whether two values are considered the same under a comparison rule. Identity asks whether two references designate the same object or entity. Ordering comparisons ask which value is earlier, smaller, or larger under a defined ordering. Languages differ in structural, reference, coercive, and strict comparison rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct comparisons are essential for conditions, searching, deduplication, state checks, sorting, and security decisions. A comparison that looks reasonable may treat different representations as equal or two equivalent structures as unequal.
understand.analogy: Two printed copies can contain the same words but are not the same physical sheet. That illustrates value equality versus identity. A rule for alphabetical ordering is a separate comparison rule.
understand.analogyLimit: Equality and identity operators vary by language and data type. Some languages overload comparisons or use structural equality by default; some permit coercion. Always consult the relevant rule.

explain.narrative: Use a comparison that answers the intended question. Primitive values may compare by value. Composite objects may compare by identity unless a language or library defines structural equality. Strict comparison avoids some implicit conversions in languages that provide it. Text comparisons may be case-sensitive or locale-aware, and numeric comparisons may need tolerances. For keys or security-sensitive checks, avoid relying on vague equality assumptions.

examples.explanation: Strict equality compares these numeric values and returns true in JavaScript.

examples.title: Text differs by case
examples.explanation: Case-sensitive string comparison sees different character sequences.

examples.title: Two separately created objects
examples.explanation: These are distinct object instances in JavaScript, so strict identity comparison is false despite similar contents.

examples.title: Same reference
examples.code: const p = {x: 1}; const q = p; p === q;
examples.explanation: Both variables refer to the same object instance, so the identity comparison is true.

examples.title: Approximate numeric comparison
examples.explanation: When values are floating-point approximations, a tolerance can express acceptable closeness.

commonMistakes: Assuming equality always checks the contents of objects.
Using coercive comparisons without understanding conversions.
Treating case-insensitive text matching as a universal rule.
Using exact floating-point equality for approximate results.
Confusing identity with equality or ordering.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Test a data rule with examples
guidedTask.instructions: Apply "Equality, Identity, and Comparison" to a small program scenario. Work through the rule and explain the result.
steps: State what the data represents and what behavior is expected.
Identify the relevant comparison, constraint, or semantic rule.
Evaluate one valid case and one invalid or edge case.
Explain the result and any side effects.
Describe a test that would prevent a regression.

independentTask.title: Independent: Build a data-rule test
independentTask.instructions: Design and test a small scenario using this lesson's concept.
requirements: State the rule or intended behavior.
Test at least one normal case.
Test one boundary, invalid, or unusual case.

hints: Describe the intended behavior before writing the condition.
Separate format/type checks from business rules.
Include a boundary or negative case in your tests.
Use exact language-specific comparison or assignment semantics.
Explain why the chosen rule is correct for this context.
